tone.quote: between Bodo and Huma links the former also to Bukur, a language which differs little from Huma. [...] (iii) Huma In connection with Huma, Fr. Giorgetti remarks that whenever I wrote 7, both Huma and Bukur in Zandeland pronounce nmgy. [...] (iv). Tones have been marked in a limited number of cases in the customary way: an acute accent for the high tone, a grave one for the low and no mark for the middle tone.
tone.locator: highlight passages for identifier sudan-notes-and, article pp. 82-99; the tone-convention sentence is section (iv) of the introductory remarks immediately before the heading ABBREVIATIONS; page numbers not recoverable
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.n_tones: 3 (high, mid, low) marked for Bodo/Huma/Kare; none stated for Bukur
tone.says: No tone statement about Bukur/Boguru. In the introductory remarks, section (iv), Santandrea states his transcription convention for the Bodo, Huma and Kare material: tones marked 'in a limited number of cases in the customary way' with acute = high, grave = low, unmarked = middle; this is a marking convention applied sparingly, not an analysis asserting three contrastive levels, and the comparative vocabulary has columns Bodo / Huma / Kare A / Kare B only (no Bukur column in the snippets). sources.note: The LSNBB team reports give short structural notes (noun classes, sometimes 'two tone levels' remarks) only for languages actually sampled in the field; the Glottolog annotation places Homa on a list page (p. 69), so the likeliest content is a bare mention/classification of Homa with Boguru, Bodo and Ngbinda, not tone data. Listed only because it is one of the two Glottolog-indexed works on Homa not previously listed here; no online text (1956 IAI print; 2017 Routledge e-reissue paywalled; archive.org search for a scan timed out).
